Some of the feedback received in the user testing pointed to feelings of frustration or boredom when the other player had more control over them. The level of control between the two players is essentially equal so that each player feels as if they need the other as much as they are needed by them.

column1: So neither player controls their own wobble or distortion. They only hear it happening
column2: so they have to listen to each other and respond. The instrument itself is built with[ Tone.js](https://tonejs.github.io/)
column3: which sits on top of the browser’s built-in Web Audio system. Each player’s sound travels through a chain of effects:

column1: Blue’s notes switch on a wobble effect (an auto filter) in yellow’s chain. Yellow’s notes switch on a distortion effect (a waveshaper) in blue’s chain.
Each player also has their own brightness
The key presses switch these effects on and off while each person plays.

The design system made it as easy as possible for first time players to understand the controls. The opening popup box established knowledge for how the instrument should be played. If this isn’t communicated clearly
column2: then players would easily become frustrated or lose interest. Keeping all of the controls within a confined area on the keyboard helped simplify what is quite a complex instrument to play well. The control variable keys (on the bottom row) are separated from the notes to avoid confusion as to what does what. The layout matches the system with the real world and each player's respective controls are a distinct colour. This quickly communicates who controls what and where the controls are
column3: to minimise players having to look down at the keyboard. It was also important to clearly visualise the keys being pressed and the effect that has on the variables

column6: so they don’t have to take their eye off what’s most important. Also
